claims.text: Pre-exposure Q235 steel naturally has a thin native oxide layer.
The native oxide provides modest passivation to Q235 steel at room temperature.
Deposited chloride salts react with the native oxide at 700–900 °C through fluxing reactions.
Chloride-induced fluxing destabilizes and breaks down the native oxide.
Breakdown of the oxide exposes the underlying Q235 steel to rapid oxidation and corrosion.
Under room-temperature, low-chloride conditions, the native oxide remains stable and acts as a kinetic corrosion barrier.
High-temperature salt exposure will rapidly compromise the oxide relative to a low-aggressiveness baseline.
High-temperature salt exposure will produce greater mass change because of accelerated oxidation.
High-temperature salt exposure will cause observable microstructural degradation relative to the unaltered baseline.
The proposed oxide-breakdown mechanism requires aggressive chloride exposure and high temperature to be present simultaneously.
At low chloride concentration or moderate temperature, the native oxide may remain protective.
Prior studies of Q235 steel are limited relative to studies of alloy or stainless steels.
Comparable mass change, microstructure, and phase composition in the high-temperature salt and room-temperature groups would falsify the proposed mechanism under the tested conditions.
